outcomes.measure_name: angular pointing error (initial movement direction error) during the adaptation phase
outcomes.higher_is_better_evidence: Their errors increased abruptly at the onset of the adaptation phase, and then gradually dropped again. Most importantly, adaptive improvement was more pronounced for young than for old subjects.
outcomes.operationalization: Median initial direction error (between movement onset and peak velocity) of center-out pointing responses per 50-s episode; the adaptation phase comprised 15 episodes with visual feedback rotated +60° (pointing episodes 6-20 in Fig. 1). Late adaptation corresponds to the final adaptation episode (episode 20); the paper reports no block-average value, only the per-episode time series in Fig. 1 plus an exponential fit whose constant term describes the asymptotic (late) error.

sources.locator: Fig. 1, pointing episode 20 (last filled/closed symbol of the adaptation phase): filled squares = old, filled triangles = young; y-axis 'angular error (deg)'
sources.quote: Fig. 1 Mean pointing errors of young (triangles) and old (squares) subjects before, during, and after exposure to rotated visual feedback. Open symbols indicate episodes where visual feedback was absent. Also shown are the standard deviations
sources.error_bar_evidence: Also shown are the standard deviations
sources.notes: Group means and SDs for each adaptation episode are available only graphically; adaptation episodes are the filled symbols between episodes 6 and 20.

sources.locator: Results, paragraph on the adaptation phase: exponential fits of the adaptation time course (constant term = asymptotic late error)
sources.quote: An exponential fit yielded y=9.92+53.51×exp(−x/5.89) for young subjects and y=29.51+29.91×exp(−x/5.13) for old subjects.
sources.notes: Fitted curve parameters, not raw group means; the additive constants (9.92 deg young, 29.51 deg old) describe the asymptotic late-adaptation error. No dispersion reported.

sources.locator: Results, ANOVA on the adaptation phase (between-factor Age, within-factor Episode)
sources.quote: significant effects were yielded for Age (F(1,22)=7.58, P<0.05), Episode (F(14,308)=41.14, P<0.001), and their interaction (F(14,308)=3.44, P<0.001)
sources.notes: Age effect spans all 15 adaptation episodes, not just the late episodes.

outcomes.measure_name: angular pointing error (after-effect) with visual feedback removed
outcomes.higher_is_better_evidence: after-effects are not a reliable measure of recalibration, because they can be artificially inflated by perseveration
outcomes.operationalization: Median initial direction error of pointing responses in the five after-effect episodes performed without visual feedback immediately after the 15 adaptation episodes (pointing episodes 21-25 in Fig. 1, plotted as open symbols). The paper reports no block average; the first after-effect episode (21) is the first available measure. Note that in Fig. 1 the after-effect errors are plotted as negative deviations (opposite in sign to the adaptation errors), so the after-effect construct corresponds to the absolute magnitude of these negative values.

sources.locator: Fig. 1, open symbols at pointing episodes 21-25 (after-effect phase); first after-effect episode = episode 21; open squares = old, open triangles = young
sources.quote: Open symbols indicate episodes where visual feedback was absent. Also shown are the standard deviations
sources.error_bar_evidence: Also shown are the standard deviations
sources.notes: Values plotted below zero (y-axis extends to −40 deg); means and SDs available only graphically.

sources.locator: Results, ANOVA on the after-effect phase (factors Age, Episode)
sources.quote: ANOVA yielded significant effects for Episode (F(4,88)=66.84, P<0.001) and the interaction (F(4,88)=3.95, P<0.01); indeed a close look at Fig. 1 reveals that the after-effect declined somewhat faster in the young group.
sources.values_in_text: Episode F(4,88)=66.84, P<0.001; Age×Episode interaction F(4,88)=3.95, P<0.01
sources.notes: No F value is printed for the main effect of Age in the after-effect phase; the text only states the after-effect was similar (age-independent) in both groups.

parsed.notes: Dataset 1 = the 12 young and 12 old experimental subjects who performed +60° rotated pointing (task_type visuomotor, perturbation +60°, 8 targets: 'visual targets appeared in one of eight possible directions'). All group means/SDs for pointing errors exist only as plotted points with SD whiskers in Fig. 1 (page 3); no table of values is provided. Other numeric locations deliberately NOT attached to the two protocol outcomes: (a) page 3, refresh-phase statistics (Age F(1,22)=13.42, P<0.01; Episode F(2,44)=6.18, P<0.01; episodes 20 vs 26 comparison Age F(1,22)=13.78, Episode F(1,22)=7.79) — this is a second, re-exposure perturbation block; (b) page 3, tracking-transfer analysis (above-baseline RMSE, Procedure F(1,43)=144,09, P<0.001) and Fig. 2 (page 4) — a different task category with control groups, and it involves a change of movement category between learning and test; (c) page 4, pooled 'magnitude of adaptation' A=(I−F)/I = 0.49±0.21 with normalized trail-making 1.78±0.55 — this comes from a supplemented sample of 54 seniors pooled with two other unpublished experiments and has no matching young-group value, so it is not a source for dataset 1; (d) page 4, trail-making times (young 27.4±7.2 s, old 42.5±6.9 s; t(22)=5.25) and normalized scores (77.55±18.40 vs 103.93±16.26; t(22)=3.72) — cognitive screening, not a protocol outcome; (e) page 2, ages (26.0±5.0 and 69.5±7.5 years).
